references.text: The Pharisees and the scribes grumbled at the disciples because Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners. This is the same type of complaint directed against Jesus in Zacchaeus' house as in Luke 5:30.
In Luke 15:1-2, the Pharisees and the scribes grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them – the same reaction as when he went into Zacchaeus' home.
Jesus was called 'a friend of tax collectors and sinners' (Luke 7:34), and the visit to Zacchaeus confirms exactly this reputation.
In Luke 7:39, the Pharisee Simon reacts when Jesus allows a sinful woman to touch him. The same pattern appears where those around condemn Jesus' association with sinners.
In Matthew 9:10-11, the Pharisees ask why Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners while he was a guest at Matthew's house. A parallel situation to the people's reaction in Zacchaeus' home.
In Mark 2:16, the scribes among the Pharisees criticize Jesus for eating with tax collectors and sinners – the same grumbling as in Jericho.
Jesus' answer to the grumbling is that the Son of Man has come to seek and save what was lost (Luke 19:10), which explains why he went into a sinner's home.
In Ezekiel 34:16, God promises to seek out the lost and bring back those who were driven away. Jesus fulfills this promise by seeking out Zacchaeus, a man everyone regarded as a sinner.

The parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector in Luke 18:9-14 shows that God justifies the humble tax collector – thematically preparing for the story of Zacchaeus and the people's condemnation of him.
